clinical_category: Chronic respiratory disease - anxiety and breathlessness interaction
blueprint_topic: Psychosocial assessment and symptom-management support for anxiety associated with chronic dyspnea
stem: A client with chronic respiratory disease says, "When I become short of breath, I panic, and then the breathing feels even harder." Which nursing response is most appropriate?

options.A: Acknowledge the anxiety as part of the symptom experience, assess its severity and safety impact, reinforce appropriate breathing or relaxation strategies, and coordinate additional psychological support when needed
options.B: Tell the client that anxiety is unrelated to chronic breathlessness and should be ignored while respiratory treatment continues
options.C: Stop evaluation of the underlying respiratory condition because the symptoms are primarily psychological
options.D: Advise the client to avoid all physical activity permanently so anxiety about breathlessness cannot recur

rationale: A is correct. Current American Thoracic Society resources describe anxiety as a common and clinically meaningful problem in chronic respiratory disease and note that breathlessness and anxious states can interact in maladaptive cycles. ATS emphasizes integrated, personalized care rather than separating psychological symptoms from respiratory care. Current ATS palliative-care guidance also identifies counseling for anxiety and difficulty breathing as a supportive intervention alongside medical treatment. B dismisses a legitimate psychosocial component. C creates a false psychological-versus-physical dichotomy and risks missing respiratory deterioration. D promotes unnecessary avoidance and deconditioning rather than individualized symptom management and appropriate activity.
educational_objective: Address anxiety associated with chronic breathlessness as a legitimate component of respiratory illness by assessing it, reinforcing safe breathing/relaxation strategies, and coordinating psychological support while continuing appropriate medical evaluation and treatment.
source_document_title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy to Manage Anxiety in Chronic Respiratory Disease; Palliative Care for People with Respiratory Disease or Critical Illness
source_version_date: Current ATS Pulmonary Rehabilitation Assembly educational resource and current ATS Patient Education palliative-care resource accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: ATS 'Cognitive Behavioral Therapy to Manage Anxiety in Chronic Respiratory Disease' → 'The impact of anxiety in chronic respiratory disease': anxiety can exacerbate symptom severity; breathlessness is closely linked with anxious states; anxiety and breathlessness may contribute to maladaptive cycles of avoidance and deconditioning. 'Moving toward a stepped, multimodal approach': psychological support should be integrated into comprehensive respiratory management. ATS 'Palliative Care for People with Respiratory Disease or Critical Illness' → chronic lung disease examples: counseling may be used to help with anxiety and difficulty breathing while medical treatment continues.
source_claim_supported: Current ATS resources directly support anxiety as a meaningful component of chronic respiratory illness, interaction between anxiety and breathlessness, and integrated psychological/breathing support alongside ongoing respiratory care.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity client-needs subcategory (6–12% of items); this item tests recognition of anxiety related to chronic illness, therapeutic communication, psychosocial assessment, coping support, and coordination of appropriate resources.
correction_summary: Substantive rebuild. The source item broadly asserted a dyspnea-anxiety physiological cycle and prescribed generic relaxation/breathing teaching from a generic ATS URL. The final item uses current exact ATS resources, tests an integrated nursing response to anxiety and breathlessness, and avoids claiming that anxiety alone explains respiratory symptoms or that one psychological technique has universal efficacy.
audit_findings: The original ATS root URL did not locate the dyspnea-anxiety management claim.
Current ATS respiratory-rehabilitation content directly describes anxiety as interacting with breathlessness and contributing to maladaptive avoidance/deconditioning cycles.
Current ATS palliative-care guidance directly supports counseling for anxiety and breathing difficulty alongside disease-directed respiratory treatment.
The final item avoids psychologizing potentially dangerous respiratory symptoms and requires continued medical assessment while supporting anxiety management.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely appropriate nursing response, no second defensible answer, no unsupported universal psychotherapy claim, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
